As I turn on my television I find a baseball game on ESPN and I say to myself, "Alright! The Colorado Rockies are playing, they're fun to watch so I'll leave 'em on." I sat down on my couch put my feet up and the remote down. The first batter I saw hit a pitch down the firstbase line and it was just foul. The fan in the front row tried to grab the rolling ball but he missed as he dropped his beer and the ball rolled further away. I laughed. On the next pitch he hit a deep fly ball towards left field, right on the warning track but the fielder caught it right in front of the big Coors Light sign. Did I mention the name of the ballpark they're playing in is Coor's Stadium? By the way, Coor's slogan is "Tap into the Rockies."

During the fifth inning there was a fight in the stands, probably drunk college kids, and a whole row got ejected. They were pretty nice seats because as soon as they got tossed the seats had been taken by fans sitting further behind them. Between innings I kept the station on because Coors has some funny adds with their "Beer Man" advertising campaign. The first add between innings was a Coors add.

I believe I see a marketing strategy here: sports fans and beer go hand in hand. Personally, I am a sports nut. I go to about ten RedSox games a year, see an average of one thousand beer drinkers, see a few drunken fights, slurred swearing and taunting, and have to stare at the scoreboard sponsored by Budweiser.

meone who has lived at home all their life. Having no curfew and
having almost total independence is a big responsibility to some
people and it takes a certain type of person to be successful in
this type of atmosphere. To me, I usually have to have some tragedy
or unfortunate experience happen to me before I realize how lucky
I am to be in this certain situation. When I'm at home, my mother
and father will always help me get through a tough situation but
now that I'm in a college over an hour away I do not have that
luxury anymore and it's a huge disadvantage to me. From now on I'm
my own boss and the only person in charge of my actions now is me.
Back in my senior year of highschool I was very scared about
living away from home. All I could think about was the
responsibility aspect of being alone, being by myself. Thoughts of
getting into trouble were always on my mind, but the more I think
about it the more I realize how much freedom I have now. No longer

Boy, what the heck happened last night, I feel like I got ran over by a truck. My head 
ached, still pounding from all the alcohol  -  almost a full bottle of Canadian Whiskey. My 
chest felt bruised along with my upper right shoulder as I was trying to remember how I got 
home the previous night, or should I say early morning. My mind drew a blank. The last 
image I could gather was sitting outside my house holding an empty bottle. My entire body 
felt a soreness that I can only compare to what a Boston Marathon runner might feel after 
completing the last step of the 26.2 mile course. Continuous questions began running 
through my head: where was my friend who was supposed to sleep over that night? What 
happened to me that made my whole body hurt? What day is it, anyway? Suddenly the 
flashback of sitting in my father's minivan listening to the radio entered my mind. The most 
intense fear I've ever known raced down my spine and made my pain all the more real. At 
that point I said a quick prayer that his minivan was still sitting in the driveway. I staggered 
out into the kitchen and my fears rang true as I gazed at a police document sitting on the 
table. The only word I remember reading was minivan. 
As tears ran down my face I crawled back into bed, just barely noticing the blood on 
my pillow. To this day I remember nothing about that almost fateful night. What 
information I got was from police reports, my father and my friend. It wasn't until a week 
later that all the pieces were finally in place and I realized just how close I came to meeting

These chickens will destroy all of the other humans in the world.

Tom, are you up to the challenge?"

My heroes are dying. There is no real way to sugar coat something as 
powerful as that. Half of the Beatles are dead. Jim Morrison, Hendrix, Joplin, 
Cobain, Presley (the young one), Marley  -  the list goes on... My daily routine 
involves checking the obituaries to see which of my favorite performers is no 
longer performing. Often when I am daydreaming in my truck or in the classroom 
I ponder who will be next? There are so many candidates to choose from but I've 
narrowed down my top five to:

1. Keith Richards 
2. Bob Dylan 
3. David Bowie 
4. Roger Waters 
5. David Crosby

It's a little sick and twisted, I know, but that's just the way my mind works. I never 
put anyone on this list from The Who, yet bass player John Entwistle passed 
away just about a month ago and drummer Keith Moon died what seems like a 
lifetime ago. You just never know when it's your time to go. My heart goes out to 
the families of anyone who has left this earth but I admit that the thought of the 
possibility of lead singer Roger Daltrey or singer and composer Pete Townshend 
dying instead of John Entwistle was deeply saddening. The defense mechanism 
of "can't wait 'til next year because they might not be here" turns on. So here I 
am at the Tweeter Center in Mansfield, Mass. I'm three hours early. Half of the 
original members of The Who are now part of the house band in Heaven, but on 
this side of the clouds the show goes on and the spirit lives for at least one more 
night. It's raining, but only on the outside.

THE COREY STORY

Tom Jensen
September 17, 2002
Advanced Writing
Professor Bochynski
---
Thirteen years ago... October. A snapshot was taken upon a mountain trail
as the dark and rich brown earth gave way to the strong forest pine trees. There
was just a tiny half-watermelon shaped patch of sky visible at the top of the
picture. I was fat - with my lil' pudding gut hanging symmetrically over the barely
zipped blue sweatshirt my mom had tried to squeeze me into that day. He was
skinny - with his blue sweatshirt tucked slimly around his waist as he showed off
his bright white NIKE sneakers. I was frowning. He was grinning. We were
eleven.

The prime of one's life is found at the age of eleven. You don't start
fighting either with or for boyfriends or girlfriends because you're still waiting for
puberty to hit. The word hobby actually means something because of all the free
time you have and school is stress free and fun as you learn about the wonderful
world of the social caste system and the Totem Pole Theory. Do whatever it
takes to not be the bottom guy and we were never the bottom guys. You never
saw such intimidation before out in the schoolyard. I have an old poem, which
reads:
I was the toughest in my class
Because the size of my ass
So Corey will catch you
And then we'll both come to get you

The gazelle and the walrus and it wasn't any petting zoo either.

BOB DYLAN:
POET, LEGEND AND PIONEER

Tom Jensen
November 15, 1999
Intro. To Poetry
Biography Sketch

Jensen1
---
Trying to sum up the career of singer/songwriter Bob Dylan in a mere five
page paper is akin to naming all the songs he wrote in alphabetical order- from
"A Fool Such as I" to "You're no Good." All anyone has to know is that he has
thirty-three songs that start with W; Need I say more?

Bob Dylan was born Robert Allen Zimmerman on May 24, 1941 in Deluth,
Minnesota. Robert Zimmerman strolled on the stage in the early sixties with a
guitar on his shoulder and a harmonica in his mouth. Music has never been the
same since. He arrived in New York city hoping to replicate his hero, folk singer
Woody Guthrie. Not only did he replicate him but he surpassed him. Dylan's
writing ability and overall talent quickly propelled him towards stardom and
legend status among the music world.

Dylan is credited with blending folk music with rock and roll and also
reconnecting country and rock. Not to mention as well as reinventing the singer
and songwriter genre. In 1964, Dylan wrote "Mr. Tambourine Man," which was
the first hit of the Byrds in 1965. And so began folk rock.

The intensity of his performances and his live in-the-studio albums
(Highway 61 Revisited and Blonde on Blonde) were a revelation. His lyrics were
analyzed, debated and quoted like no pop music before them. "I consider myself
a poet first and a musician second. I live like a poet and I'll die like a poet." -
Dylan said in 1978 according to "If There's An Original Thought Out There I

BOB DYLAN

In my opinion there are two different forms in which poetry can be
categorized into - poetry that is a pleasure to the eyes (as in Shakespeare or
Edgar Allen Poe) and poetry which is a pleasure to the ears (as in music and
opera). Simply put there is written poems and songs. The poetry which is
included in both categories is often the most challenging. It takes more skill and
more of a mastery of both language and its sounds. I have never been attracted
to poetry in only word form - I appreciate beats and percussions. It is for this
reason I decided to choose Bob Dylan : Master wordsmith, master musician.

Tom Jensen
January 27, 1999
Creative Writing

A Hard Rain's Gonna Fall

The smoke from a half lit cigarette waves aimlessly through the air. A light brown guitar sits in the corner awaiting the delicate touch of its master. Three empty notebooks sit atop the table curiously wondering what will fill their blank pages. Will there be small sketches of beautiful young women or perhaps some silly verses about how everybody must get stoned? An old weathered, green chair, still feeling the pain of a dropped cigarette, reminices about the time it's owner, the master, once sat for what seemed like an eternity trying to capture the soul of a man named Hollis Brown. An old, rusty razor lays, forgotten, in a corner clutching on to one last piece of cocaine. A broken guitar string sits beneath a pile of trash still humming the melody of what it prays comes true in "Forever Young", and in the state of mind that it will never be thrown away.

A familiar face appears from behind a closed door. All of the objects in the room experience a buzz of excitement. Perhaps one of them will receive their master's attention, if even only for an instant. The master sits upon the green chair and sighs. "Must be another sad love song", the chair thinks to itself. The razor, on the other hand says, "I think he's angry at the world, I hope he's not as angry as that 'Masters of war' song...You know, the one that goes:

And I hope that you die
And you're death'll come soon
I will follow your casket
In the pale afternoon
And I'll watch while you're lowered
Down to your deathbed

It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Bleeding)

Tom Jensen
Literary Criticism
February 11, 2004
Dr. Sheehan
---
Connection to 
formalism

Friedrich Nietzsche once wrote, "The individual has always had to struggle to 
keep from being overwhelmed by the tribe. If you try it, you will be lonely often, and 
sometimes frightened. But no price is too high to pay for the privilege of owning 
yourself."

At the risk of being guilty of the heresy of paraphrase, I do not think that even Mr.
Bob Dylan himself would argue that his intentions in the creation of his illuminating song 
entitled, "It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Bleeding)," were to emphasize the importance of 
individualism while rejecting the herd mentality so prevalent in American culture. This 
piece has clearly didactic intentions. But this critique is not concerned with the author's 
intentions, nor is it interested in giving a history lesson on 1965, the year this song was 
first heard. And for that matter, there will be no talk of hippies or crew cuts,

individualism and also acts as one of the motifs that help unite this piece. Your average 
person would probably name this song: I'm in trouble ma (get me to the hospital, 
QUICK!). Hence the title further emphasizes the fact that individualism is the key to 
freedom from the 'rat race' that is society, or rather, the collective herd mentality of 
society. Two motifs are present throughout this poem  -  the first concerns itself with

AVOIDING MY OLD HOBBY by Tom Jensen

As the slow and steady rain falls from the sky down onto the ground I am awakened by the aroma of my father's coffee as it slowly seeps beneath my door and finally reaches my nose. Upon waking and gathering my senses another thought fills my head. If the morning coffee is ready it must be time for my waking routine of having a cup of hot Java in one hand (with cream and sugar, of course) and a newly lit cigarette in the other. My life is just a series of routine after routine. It is my belief that each person's series of routines either makes or breaks their life, and makes up their lifestyle.

We are all creatures of habit, whether we like it or not. My unfortunate luck is that I always seem to get stuck with the bad habits rather than the good ones. You see, a majority of my bad habits, or routines, are all interconnected. Imagine a chain link fence or perhaps a sweater, each individual fabric or link holds all the others in place. Even if one or two individual structures are removed the form, or routine, will remain the same. This interconnectedness is what makes the structure, in my case the routine, the same. The coffee leads to a cigarette and. the cigarette leads to an even greater evil: drugs and alcohol.

My dilemma is that to take only a part out will not change the structure and therefore do no good. There will still be links to the past. With links to the past still remaining it becomes much harder to change a daily pattern. Not only must the chain link fence be disassembled but its very foundation be torn from the ground. It takes a very strong man to do that - to completely change a lifestyle. In order to achieve a goal of this magnitude the right substitutes must be chosen and a new foundation must be poured.
